The upside is real, but it is mostly **variance reduction**.

A capable model can sometimes produce an excellent zero-shot answer. The problem is that without enough grounding, its search space is enormous. Giving it authoritative context, explicit interfaces, schemas, examples, and deterministic tools collapses that space:

```text
weakly constrained model
→ thousands of plausible interpretations
→ one gets selected probabilistically

well-grounded model
→ a handful of legitimate interpretations
→ much higher first-pass success rate
```

That is why MCP-style setups can feel dramatically better. The useful part isn't some magic property of MCP; it's that the model gets a **persistent, machine-readable action surface**: named tools, descriptions, schemas, resources, and sometimes server-level instructions. Instead of hoping the model remembers, “When this kind of thing happens, go read X,” the relevant capability is sitting directly in its tool-selection environment every turn.

And that explains the contrast you've noticed:

**Custom instruction:**  
“Always consult this thing when doing X.”

The model still has to interpret that instruction, remember that X applies, decide that retrieval is required, pick the right retrieval mechanism, and actually execute it.

**Dedicated tool/MCP operation:**  
`get_authoritative_context_for_x()`

Now there's one highly salient action whose very existence tells the model what to do.

That's a much stronger affordance.

Where it becomes ridiculous from the user side is when you have to build increasingly elaborate machinery simply to achieve:

> “Before answering this class of question, read the authoritative material I already gave you.”

You shouldn't need a state machine, evaluator, retrieval gate, verifier, encryption transport, and custom tool server just to make that behavior dependable.

The more useful design principle for what you're doing is probably **not** “put every instruction into custom instructions.” It's:

```text
Keep model instructions small.

Put authoritative knowledge in retrievable resources.

Expose one or a few very obvious operations that retrieve the right resources.

Make required retrieval deterministic for tasks where missing it would invalidate the answer.
```

That gives you most of the MCP effect without turning the prompt into a constitution.

Also, one distinction matters: **MCP itself does not inherently require replacing Google Drive, GitHub, or other tools.** MCP is just a protocol for exposing tools/resources. If a particular host configuration makes an MCP setup mutually exclusive with other connectors, that's a limitation of that host/integration arrangement, not an intrinsic MCP requirement.

The ideal environment would let you have both:

```text
Your control MCP
    ├─ canonical instructions
    ├─ context resolver
    ├─ verifier
    └─ task-specific operations

PLUS

native connectors
    ├─ Google Drive
    ├─ Gmail
    ├─ GitHub
    └─ Calendar
```

Then your MCP acts as the **control plane**, while the other connectors remain the **data/action plane**.

That, to me, is the actual upside of “helping” the AI: not spoon-feeding it answers, but changing the environment so there are fewer opportunities for it to make an avoidable stupid decision.

Yes. That can be a **real host-level limitation**, even though it is not an MCP limitation.

The distinction is:

- **MCP protocol:** nothing about MCP says “if this server is present, all other tools disappear.”
- **ChatGPT tool/runtime configuration:** the host decides which tool surfaces are exposed to the model for a particular message or mode.

OpenAI's current documentation actually says ChatGPT can select **one or more apps for a single message** and can invoke multiple first-party and third-party apps in the same prompt. citeturn357644search0 So the intended current product behavior is not “custom MCP excludes everything else.”

But that does **not** invalidate what you've observed. If, in a particular developer-mode configuration, selecting your draft MCP causes Drive/GitHub/plugin tools to vanish from the active tool set, then the model literally cannot use those tools in that invocation. Trying a dozen fresh chats would give you the same result because it's the **tool surface supplied by the host**, not the model merely deciding not to call them.

That's also why it can look like hallucination. The model may say:

> “I can use Google Drive…”

because it understands conceptually that ChatGPT has Drive integration, while its **actual current invocation does not contain a Drive tool**. Then it starts improvising explanations for why it can't perform the action.

There are also explicit mode restrictions today. For example, OpenAI says custom apps aren't usable by Agent mode, and developer-mode MCP availability varies by plan/client; custom MCP apps are web-only in the documented full-MCP setup. citeturn357644search0

So I would characterize your experience as:

```text
Your MCP is not replacing the other tools by protocol.

The ChatGPT host is sometimes constructing an invocation
whose active tool set contains your developer MCP
but excludes the other connector/plugin tools.
```

And **that is a significant architectural problem for what you're building**, because your control MCP works precisely because it is highly salient and reliable—but if obtaining that reliability means losing Drive, GitHub, or other native tools, you've traded orchestration reliability for capability.

The ideal behavior documented by OpenAI is actually what you want: **your MCP + other apps in the same prompt**. If your particular developer-mode environment consistently prevents that, I would treat it as a product/runtime limitation or bug rather than something you're configuring incorrectly unless there's another workspace restriction involved. citeturn357644search0

Right. In that setup, it really can become a wash.

If your **MCP is the thing enforcing the controller logic anyway**, then giving that same MCP access to Google Drive and GitHub means you no longer care much whether ChatGPT exposes its native Drive/GitHub connectors in that mode.

The architecture becomes:

```text
ChatGPT
  ↓
your MCP
  ├─ controller logic
  ├─ canonical instructions
  ├─ Google Drive access
  ├─ GitHub access
  ├─ verification
  └─ task routing
```

instead of:

```text
ChatGPT
  ├─ your MCP
  ├─ native Google Drive connector
  ├─ native GitHub connector
  └─ other plugins
```

For what you're doing, the first architecture has some real advantages:

- **One control surface.** The model doesn't have to choose among five semantically overlapping tools.
- **You define the semantics.** Your MCP can say exactly what “read the authoritative file,” “submit to evaluator,” or “write processing branch” means.
- **You can force ordering.** Retrieve context first, then execute, then verify.
- **You can normalize APIs.** Drive, GitHub, Sheets, whatever can all look like a consistent set of operations.
- **You can log everything.** Tool calls, source reads, writes, verification results.
- **You can make bad paths impossible.** If the model shouldn't write plaintext to GitHub, simply don't expose an operation that allows that.

The cost is mainly on your side: authentication, API maintenance, token refresh, permissions, retries, schema changes, and keeping the MCP healthy. But if you're already building agent controllers on top of Drive and GitHub, that work is happening anyway.

So your practical conclusion makes sense:

> If developer MCP mode knocks out native tools, but the MCP itself can reach those systems, then the lost native connectors are mostly a UX loss rather than a capability loss.

And in your case, the MCP may actually be **more reliable** because the model sees one purpose-built interface instead of having to infer which generic connector action to use.

Yes. What you’ve converged on is less “an MCP with a bunch of fixed tools” and more **a programmable control plane for the agent**.

The pieces now line up pretty cleanly:

```text
ChatGPT / model
      │
      ▼
Your MCP
      │
      ├─ mandatory controller/rule context
      ├─ arbitrary JavaScript execution request
      ├─ persistent state/storage access
      ├─ GitHub access
      ├─ Google Drive / Sheets access
      └─ verifier/controller operations
             │
             ▼
      GitHub Actions / Node.js
             │
             ├─ execute generated JS
             ├─ read/write persistent data
             ├─ run deterministic checks
             ├─ call APIs
             └─ return structured result
```

That gets you the combination you were looking for:

- **Model writes the program.**
- **A durable runtime executes it.**
- **Storage survives ChatGPT containers.**
- **The runtime can access external systems.**
- **Return schemas constrain what comes back.**
- **MCP makes the whole thing look authoritative and tool-like to the model.**

And the big breakthrough from Node/GitHub Actions is exactly what you described: you no longer need to keep asking the agent to inspect and reconstruct some external runtime before doing anything. The program it just wrote can run immediately in the workflow environment.

That removes this entire class of garbage:

```text
Does this runtime support X?
Where is dependency Y?
Is this Apps Script compatible?
Can I execute this here?
Let me inspect the environment.
Let me verify the source.
```

Instead:

```text
write JS
→ execute JS
→ inspect return value
```

That is a much tighter agent loop.

## The MCP piece you're missing

The most valuable thing your MCP can do may not even be the arbitrary-code executor. It may be the **context admission contract**.

Something like:

```text
Any interaction with this MCP must begin with:

1. Load controller rules.
2. Return controller rules to the model.
3. Only then expose/perform requested operation.
```

So rather than trusting:

> “Before using this tool, please remember to read the rulebook.”

the MCP can enforce:

```text
tool request
    ↓
MCP server loads current rulebook
    ↓
tool response contains rulebook + operation result
    ↓
model cannot receive operation result without also receiving rules
```

That is materially stronger.

You can even formalize every response:

```json
{
  "controller": {
    "rules_version": "abc123",
    "rules": { "...": "..." }
  },
  "execution": {
    "status": "PASS",
    "result": { "...": "..." }
  }
}
```

Then **the rules are part of the tool protocol**, not a behavioral suggestion.

## Arbitrary execution can also be one generic MCP tool

You don't need fifty MCP methods if you don't want them.

Conceptually:

```json
{
  "name": "execute_javascript",
  "arguments": {
    "source": "return ...",
    "input": {...}
  }
}
```

Your server can then dispatch that to Node/GitHub Actions/App Script, depending on how you implement the backend.

The model effectively gets:

> “If you can express the operation in JavaScript, you can perform it.”

That is a very different capability surface from ordinary fixed-function connectors.

And modules can stay persistent:

```text
modules/
  github.js
  drive.js
  sheets.js
  storage.js
  verifier.js
```

The generated program can call those instead of rebuilding API mechanics every time.

So an execution might conceptually be:

```js
const files = await drive.search("Agents.md");
const rules = await drive.read(files[0]);
const result = evaluate(input, rules);
return result;
```

while your MCP/runtime supplies `drive`, `github`, etc.

## And this explains why your earlier systems kept evolving

You were solving several different problems that initially looked like one problem:

```text
ephemeral execution
persistent storage
external API access
context reliability
agent compliance
verification
```

Apps Script addressed persistence/execution.

Sheets addressed state.

GitHub addressed durable code + automation.

Node removed much of the runtime friction.

Return schemas addressed model-output control.

Your evaluator addressed correctness.

MCP addresses **tool salience and mandatory context admission**.

Those pieces actually fit together.

The strongest version of the system is probably not “MCP replaces everything.” It is:

> **MCP is the agent-facing operating interface; GitHub/Node/Drive/Sheets are implementation infrastructure behind it.**

Then ChatGPT doesn't have to understand your infrastructure every time. It only has to understand your MCP contract.

And that gets directly at the problem you've been fighting: instead of repeatedly persuading the model to behave as though it has an operating procedure, **you give it an operating environment that makes the procedure the default path.**
